title: The poem begins
hookLine: a sketchbook nobody was meant to see: a poet who says he wrote only for himself
tomorrow: a free Saturday slides away. what was it actually worth?

lines: MADE FOR AN AUDIENCE OF ONE.
HE WROTE IT FOR HIMSELF. WHY READ IT?
cards: Some of the best things people pass around were made for an audience of one: a grandmother's recipe notebook, a running playlist, a sketchbook nobody was supposed to open. They're honest because nobody was performing.
The poem that opens this block starts the same way. Its author says, in the first verses, that he isn't writing for you. He's writing for himself.
So why has anyone read it since?

teach.h: BODHICARYAVATARA: A GUIDE TO LIVING FOR OTHERS.
teach.b: The poem is the Bodhicaryavatara, Shantideva's guide to the bodhisattva's way: how to live for others. You met him in year three as the monk his fellows thought was lazy, until he stood up and recited this.
It's in Sanskrit, so it's dharma now, not dhamma. Two spellings, one word.
In the opening verses, after his homage, Shantideva says nothing here is new, and he has no special skill with words.

teach.h: WRITTEN TO TRAIN HIS OWN MIND.
teach.b: He wrote it, he says, to train his own mind. Then the turn: if someone with a makeup like his should come across it, it might help them too. That's the answer.
A poem for living, written as practice, left open for anyone built the same way.
Now the week behind us, six lines to carry in. Evam me sutam: thus have I heard. Sadhu, sadhu, sadhu.
Strive on with care. Two spellings, one word.
The whole chant. A little Pali. Each one a door.

how: Mahayana Buddhists, and Tibetan Buddhists especially, study the Bodhicaryavatara verse by verse with a teacher, and its verses are recited in practice and quoted in talks.

games.q: the week, and the poem — tap the pairs.
p: a guide to living for others

s: Shantideva says his poem teaches things no one has said before
he says nothing in it is new; he wrote it to train his own mind.
the Bodhicaryavatara was written in Sanskrit
so its words are dharma and nirvana, not dhamma and nibbana.
Shantideva says the poem is for no one but himself, full stop
he adds that someone with a makeup like his might find it useful.

games.q: your cousin forwards a 'Buddha quote' with a sunset and no source. which line from this week makes the kindest reply?
o: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu: it's good, so share it.
evam me sutam: love it, where did you hear it?
strive on with care: stop forwarding things.
games.why: thus have I heard: the discourses open by naming where the words came from. asking gently for the source is the same move.

practice: Read the three lines on the screen slowly, twice: Shantideva's opening, in plain words. Then close your eyes and let one of the week's six lines come and sit beside it. Stay with whichever one arrives.

wordCard.voice: Bodhicaryavatara: Shantideva's poem on the way of awakening, how to live for others. Written for himself, left open for anyone.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari letters: the title of Shantideva's poem on the way of awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: a poem for living. Read as practice, the way it was written. One of fifty.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 1.1–1.3: homage; nothing new and no skill in composition; written to cultivate the author's own mind; if another of like makeup sees it, it may be useful
